extracted.intended_audience: immigration practitioners, adjudicators/consular officers, DHS rulewriters, and public commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and factors used by DHS and courts to determine whether an alien is a 'public charge' for purposes of inadmissibility, including statutory text, agency regulations, case law precedents, and definitions of relevant benefits and conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primarily-dependent (more-than-50%) bright-line standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'primarily dependent' (more-than-50-percent dependence) standard creates a bright-line rule for public charge determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble notes that the primarily dependent standard creates a bright line but acknowledges that many individuals whose receipt of public benefits falls below that standard may still lack self-sufficiency. Circuits have disagreed about whether the primarily dependent standard is embedded in the statute or whether the statute grants the executive broad discretion to consider a non-finite list of factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the alien's circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The determination of whether an alien is likely to become a public charge is 'a prediction based upon the totality of the alien's circumstances at the time he or she applies for an immigrant visa or admission to the United States.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Matter of Perez and Matter of A-: decision must be based on the totality of circumstances; requires more than a showing of a possibility that the alien will require public support. Examples and case law underline considering contemporaneous facts (employment, funds, family support, local conditions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional factors to consider in public-charge determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors include age, health and physical condition, physical or mental defects affecting earning capacity, vocation, past record of employment, current employment, offer of employment, number of dependents, existing conditions in the United States, sufficient funds or assurances of support by relatives or friends, bond or undertaking, or any specific circumstances reasonably tending to show that the burden of supporting the alien is likely to be cast on the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from Matter of Martinez-Lopez and other precedent; the preamble cites these as traditional considerations that adjudicators have historically used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Past receipt of public benefits is not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that an alien has been on welfare or received public benefits does not, by itself, establish that he or she is likely to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple cases (Matter of Perez, Matter of A-, etc.) emphasize that prior benefit receipt may be considered as evidence but is not alone sufficient to find likely future dependence. Agencies may still consider evidence of past benefit receipt as one factor among many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term institutionalization as ground for public charge
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-term institutionalization at government expense means government assistance for long-term institutionalization (in Medicaid limited to institutional services under section 1905(a)) received by a beneficiary, including in a nursing facility or mental health institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term institutionalization does not include imprisonment for conviction of a crime or institutionalization for short periods for rehabilitation purposes. This is the kind of institutional care historically treated as evidence of being a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Which public benefits count (categories and examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public benefits referenced include Supplemental Security Income (SSI), Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF), Federal, State, or local cash benefit programs for income maintenance (General Assistance), SNAP, Medicaid (including per-capita expenditure context), Section 8 housing assistance, and other federal/state/local programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble cites program statutes and administrative sources (e.g., HHS overview, HUD Section 8, SSA statistics) and compares per-enrollee expenditures to illustrate fiscal impact. It also notes the 2019 rule's explicit exclusions for certain categories (e.g., benefits for enlisted servicemembers and certain children).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions from consideration of certain benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain benefits are statutorily or rulewise excluded from consideration in public-charge determinations (e.g., benefits authorized under 8 U.S.C. 1641(c) for certain battered aliens; benefits received by enlisted service members or their families under prior rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble explains past regulatory exclusions (2019 Final Rule examples) and statutory protections that prohibit consideration of some benefits for specific protected categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of Support (INA 213A) may be considered but is not mandatory
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute permits, but does not require, consideration of a sufficient Affidavit of Support under section 213A of the INA when required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites INA sec. 212(a)(4)(B)(ii) and notes that sponsors' affidavits are enforceable under INA sec. 213A; discusses sponsor support rules including special lower threshold for active-duty sponsors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sponsor affidavit and enforceability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 551 of IIRIRA created INA sec. 213A and specified requirements for a sponsor's affidavit, including making it enforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes statutory specifics, including exceptions such as a sponsor on active duty needing to show support equal to at least 100 percent of the Federal poverty line for certain petitions; references legislative history emphasizing agencies could seek reimbursement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited circumstances for re-evaluating inadmissibility after admission
rubrics_metrics.description: Once DHS makes an inadmissibility determination and an alien is granted admission or adjustment of status, DHS generally does not re-evaluate inadmissibility, except in narrow statutory circumstances (for example, where an LPR becomes an applicant for admission under INA 101(a)(13)(C)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble explains exceptions (abandonment of LPR status, long absences, illegal activity) and situates how naturalization or lawful admission assessments may nonetheless consider admissibility at time of admission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disability cannot be the sole determinative factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Disability alone shall not be the sole determinative factor for a finding of inadmissibility on public charge grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble references litigation under the Rehabilitation Act and states DHS believes an explicit regulatory prohibition on using disability as the sole determinant is unnecessary because the law already precludes such consideration; nevertheless, prior rules included such a provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjudicator/consular officer discretion ('in the opinion of')
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute and precedent indicate that determinations about whether someone is likely to become a public charge rest within the discretion of consular officers or the Commissioner ('in the opinion of'), placing borderline adverse determinations largely beyond judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Matter of Harutunian and other cases underscoring subjective adjudicator discretion for visa purposes and the historical practice of deferring to official opinion in borderline cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial approaches and circuit divergence on statutory meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have taken differing approaches: some circuits emphasize plain text and historical meaning of 'public charge' (imposing a floor requiring substantial dependency), while others emphasize executive discretion to consider a broader, non-finite list of factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses Circuit decisions (Second, Fourth, Seventh, Ninth Circuits) and notes how the Seventh Circuit found a 'floor inherent in the words' requiring a degree of dependency beyond temporary receipt of benefits; cites cases and the litigation history of the 2019 rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency interpretive deference post-Loper Bright (Chevron overruled)
rubrics_metrics.description: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo overruled Chevron deference for agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes and acknowledged that courts, rather than agencies, determine the best interpretation of ambiguous statutory language. Agency interpretations may still be persuasive under Skidmore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble explains that while Chevron is overruled, agency views within their expertise may still carry Skidmore-type persuasive weight depending on the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold requirement of 'some specific circumstance' for finding likely public charge
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute and case law require more than a showing of possibility; some specific circumstance (such as mental or physical disability, advanced age, or other facts) reasonably tending to show that the burden of supporting the alien is likely to be cast on the public must be present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Matter of Perez, Matter of Martinez-Lopez, and related precedent emphasizing that specific circumstances, not mere possibility, are necessary to support an inadmissibility finding.
